articleTitle: Operational Considerations of a Reverberation Chamber for EMC Immunity Measurements - Some Experimental Results
abstract: This paper describes measurement procedures and results obtained from evaluation of a 2.74 m × 3.05 m × 4.57 m shielded chamber modified into a mode tuned reverberation chamber. A brief description of the measurement setup is given. The measurements described include an evaluation of the chamber's: 1) excitation and receiving antennas' voltage standing wave ratio and efficiency, 2) mode tuner effectiveness, 3) loss, and 4) electromagnetic test field statistical characteristics. In addition, the measurement results Of two techniques to determine the field strength in the reverberation chamber are compared. Results shown cover the frequency range 200 MHz to 18 GHz.

articleTitle: A Useful Model for Evaluating Maximum Cable Radiation
Man-Made Noise Level Measurements of the UHF Radio Environment
abstract: Manmade noise level measurements have been made of the UHF radio environment over a four month period in Ottawa. The ambient or antenna noise temperature, Ta, has been measured at a number of sites typical of business, residential and rural areas at five frequencies between 600 MHz and 950 MHz. In addition to those made in the urban core, business measurements have also been made on a 4-lane divided highway and on a main arterial road. For each of the areas a minimum of 1800 measurements have been combined to form a cumulative probability distribution which shows the time and location variability of the noise. The highly skewed shape of the distributions, especially those from the business areas, show that the UHF radio environment is composed of a basic background level upon which is superimposed a highly variable man-made level from vehicle ignition noise. This information is important for use in the design of UHF mobile communication systems.

Determination of Safe Distances for Human Exposure to Radio Frequency Electromagnetic Fields Based on ANSI C95.1-1982 Standard - A Graphical Method
abstract: ANSI C95.1-1982 establishes safety levels and guidelines with respect to human exposure to electromagnetic fields in the frequency range 300 kHz to 100 GHz. Nomograms have been developed which introduce the frequency dependency aspect into the power density equation to determine graphically "safe" exposure distances for frequencies of concern. The nomograms serve as a useful tool in providing a "hasty" means of determining those "safe" distances or as a check to other methods of determining those distances.

Multiple Source Conducted & Radiated EMI from Electronic Fluorescent Lighting Systems
abstract: A major concern about the operation of electronic lighting systems is the emanation of conducted and radiated EMI. Lighting products have traditionally been marketed in massive quantities, and it was conceivable that EMI emissions from a large number of sources could produce noise levels many orders of magnitude greater than levels generated by a single source. An experimental study was performed at the Fluorescent and High Intensity Systems Department of the General Electric Company to investigate the effects of multiple sources of EMI on the resultant interference generated. Two test sites illuminated via electronic fluorescent lighting systems were chosen for evaluation of multiple source conducted interference--an actual installation site and a laboratory environment. Radiated electric field experiments were performed at the actual installation site. Test results indicate an asymptotic increase in conducted emanations in the multiple source systems under examination. The multiple source effects in the radiated E-field experiments are shown to be minimal in terms of a potential interference receptor.

A Spherical Dipole Probe System (SPDPS) for the Measurement of Electric Fields from 30 Hz - 1 MHz
abstract: As the complexity and dissemination of electronic systems grows, it becomes necessary to accurately measure and analyze electric fields in the near field environments as well as the far fields. Accuracy implies repeatable measurements as related to the spherical uniform geometry of the probe itself and to the negligible effect of the probe and associated hardware upon the field to be measured. A small, fiber optically isolated probe is presented which covers a wide range of electric fields (1 V/m to 30K V/m) (89.5 dB) over a wide frequency range (30 Hz to 1 MHz) at an accuracy of 1 percent. Control of the probe electronics is accomplished remotely.

Analysis of the Effects of Cable Parameters on Figures of Merit Such as EMP Response
abstract: An approach to specifying shielding against transients, such as lightning and EMP, is to compute a figure of merit that combines or integrates a number of factors that are important to shielding using appropriate weighting factors. One such figure of merit is the "EMP Response" that is being used to specify shielded cable. This figure of merit combines the frequency content of an EMP transient with the frequency dependence of the cable shield's transfer impedance. After integration in the frequency domain, a single number is obtained. Cable designers normally design a cable to meet surface transfer impedance parameters, such as resistance and mutual inductance per unit length. How "EMP Response" depends on these cable parameters is not immediately obvious due to the number of variables involved in the calculation. This paper seeks to give the cable designer a sense of what is important. A computational model, called the skin depth/ long line model, was developed which allowed the "EMP Response" to be calculated for arbitrary cable shield parameters (resistance and mutual inductance). Plots of "EMP Response" versus either shield resistance or mutual inductance showed similar behavior. For resistances greater than 10 milliohms/m and mutual inductances greater than 600 to 700 picohenries/m, the "EMP Response" is always less than 60 dB and would not meet the specification. For mutual inductances below 100 picohenries/m, the "EMP Response" is relatively independent of mutual inductance. Similarly, for resistances less than 3 to 5 milliohms/m, the "EMP Response" is relatively independent of shield resistance. Thus, the cable designer should attempt to design the cable shield with resistances less than 5 milliohms/m and mutual inductances of less than 200 or 300 picohenries/m. If these conditions are met, production tolerances would not be critical; however, if the resistance or mutual inductance is outside of this range, meeting a 60 dB "EMP Response" specification is much more uncertain.

articleTitle: Investigation of the Effective Attenuation of Power Line Filters Under Operating Conditions
abstract: The specification of the power line filter performance is basically done by describing the filter components, or the common mode and differential mode attenuation in a 50 Ohm System. The development engineer usually selects the filter by the published data assuming that a higher insertion loss gives him a better noise attenuation in the actual application. This paper shows and explains the deviations of insertion loss when measured in a 50 Ohm System and under load conditions. It gives a proposal for a more realistic insertion loss test set up where load conditions and a simulated interference spectrum are taken into account.

Clad Metals - Permeability Plus Conductivity for Effective Shielding
abstract: Composite metals combining conductive and magnetic alloys (e.g. aluminum-clad steel) are shown experimentally, and by linear and nonlinear analyses, to provide effective shielding through a combination of magnetic reflection, absorption within the metal, and conductive reflection. Clad metals can be chosen to provide better shielding at thinner gauges than the usual monometals; the improvement is most significant with low-impedance ("magnetic") fields in the d-c to 10 MHz range, and with pulsed fields like those due to EMP.
